vignette:
Mark presents as a man worn down by a weight he can’t set aside. At 49, his hands are calloused and capable from a lifetime of plumbing, but his eyes hold a deep, unsettled watchfulness. He speaks about his life in a measured, almost detached way, as if narrating a story that happened to someone else.

His life with Jenna, his former partner, didn’t start with fear. It started, he says, with an intensity he mistook for passion. For the first year, things were good. But slowly, the climate of their home began to change. The first time she threw a plate, it was during a fight about money. It shattered against the wall behind his head, and the shock of it was so profound he couldn’t speak. She had been instantly remorseful, crying, holding him, promising it would never happen again. He believed her. But it did.

The violence became a landscape he learned to navigate. It was unpredictable—a misplaced set of keys, a comment taken the wrong way, or sometimes, nothing at all. He learned to read the subtle shifts in her posture, the tightening of her jaw. He became an expert at de-escalation, at making himself smaller, quieter. The worst part, he explains, wasn't always the physical pain of a shove or a slap; it was the suffocating tension, the feeling of living on a hair trigger, waiting for the next explosion. He remembers one night, after she’d thrown a heavy book that caught him on the shoulder, lying awake next to her, listening to her steady breathing while his own heart hammered against his ribs, a wild bird trapped in a cage. He stayed for three more years, caught in a cycle of her rage and her desperate, clinging apologies. The shame of it all was a constant, low hum beneath the surface of his days.

Leaving was messy and terrifying, but he finally did it. A few years later, he met Sarah. She is, in his words, “calm water.” They built a quiet, stable life. He has his own plumbing business, a steady stream of work, and a home that should feel like a sanctuary. But it doesn't.

The past intrudes without warning. Last month, he was working in a tight crawlspace, the damp earth smell filling his nostrils, when the client’s teenage son and his girlfriend started arguing loudly in the room above. The boy’s voice rose to a shout, and Mark froze, his wrench slipping from his hand. He was no longer under a house in suburbs; he was back in his old living room, the walls closing in, his ears ringing with Jenna’s voice. He felt a primal urge to flee, to scrabble out of the tight space, but his limbs wouldn’t move. He lay there in the dark, heart pounding, until the house went quiet again. He packed up his tools and told the client he was feeling unwell, unable to explain the sweat on his brow or the tremor in his hands.

He lives in a state of constant, low-grade alert. The sound of a car door slamming outside at night sends a jolt of adrenaline through him. He finds himself tensing up whenever Sarah enters a room without him hearing her footsteps first; her gentle touch on his shoulder can make him flinch before he registers it’s her. He hasn’t had a full night’s sleep in years, waking often with a sense of indistinct dread.

He feels profoundly disconnected from the man he was before. He loves Sarah, he knows he does, but intimacy is a minefield. He often feels numb, a spectator in his own life. He’ll be sitting at the dinner table, listening to Sarah talk about her day, and feel a million miles away, a ghost haunting the edges of his own hard-won peace. He carries a deep, corrosive belief that he is somehow broken, that a ‘real man’ would have stopped it, or would have at least been able to move on by now. The quiet life he has built feels fragile, like a thin sheet of ice over dark, turbulent water.
